text: Due to increased regulations on the advertising and marketing of commercial tobacco, smoking in movies remains one of the last avenues for tobacco companies to advertise their products to captive youth audiences. Longitudinal research has demonstrated that commercial tobacco images in movies recruit new smokers and subsequently lead to an increase in preventable tobacco-related deaths and disease. Research has indicated that a higher exposure to tobacco imagery in movies increases the uptake of smoking among youth and undermines tobacco prevention efforts. In Ontario, between 2004 and 2014, 86 percent of new release movies containing tobacco imagery were youth-rated, a much higher proportion than in the U.S. (54 percent). As a result, Ontario youth had greater exposure to on-screen tobacco imagery than their U.S. counterparts. In Ontario alone, this will result in an estimated 185,000…

The Board of Health: 1. Endorsed action on smoke-free movies to reduce youth exposure to on-screen smoking. 2. Requested the Ontario Minister of Government and Consumer Services to designate new movies with smoking and tobacco product placement an 18A rating. 3. Directed that the Board of Health's decision be forwarded to the Ontario Film Review Board for information.
